Chapter 4 Energy and Power - Worked Examples

ELEC 103 · Electrical Skills and Techniques
20 problems
We’ll work through these together in class.
Problem 1
Ch. 4 — Power from Energy and Time
A heating element uses $W = 4500\ \text{J}$ of energy in $t = 60\ \text{s}$. Find its power.
Find the power $P$ in watts.
75.0 W
Step 1Identify the given values: $W = 4500\ \text{J}$ and $t = 60\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Use the definition of power: $P = W/t$.
Step 3Substitute the values: $$P = \frac{4500\ \text{J}}{60\ \text{s}}$$
Step 4Simplify, noting $1\ \text{J/s} = 1\ \text{W}$: $P = 75.0\ \text{W}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $W = 4500\ \text{J}$, $t = 60\ \text{s}$. Power is the rate at which energy is used: $$P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{4500\ \text{J}}{60\ \text{s}} = 75.0\ \text{J/s} = 75.0\ \text{W}$$ Since $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$, the element dissipates $P = 75.0\ \text{W}$.
Problem 2
Ch. 4 — Energy Cost in Kilowatt-Hours
A $1200\ \text{W}$ space heater runs $4.0\ \text{h}$ per day for 30 days. Electricity costs 0.14 dollars per kWh. Find the cost of running the heater for the month.
Find the monthly cost in dollars.
20.2 dollars
Step 1Convert the power to kilowatts: $1200\ \text{W} = 1.2\ \text{kW}$.
Step 2Find the total operating time: $t = 4.0\ \text{h/day} \times 30 = 120\ \text{h}$.
Step 3Compute the energy: $$W = Pt = 1.2\ \text{kW} \times 120\ \text{h} = 144\ \text{kWh}$$
Step 4Multiply by the rate: $144\ \text{kWh} \times 0.14$ dollars/kWh $= 20.16 \approx 20.2$ dollars.
Worked Solution
Given: $P = 1200\ \text{W}$, $4.0\ \text{h/day}$, 30 days, rate $= 0.14$ dollars/kWh. Convert power to kilowatts: $$P = 1200\ \text{W} = 1.2\ \text{kW}$$ Total time: $$t = 4.0\ \text{h/day} \times 30\ \text{days} = 120\ \text{h}$$ Energy: $$W = P t = 1.2\ \text{kW} \times 120\ \text{h} = 144\ \text{kWh}$$ Cost: $$144\ \text{kWh} \times 0.14\ \frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{kWh}} = 20.16 \approx 20.2\ \text{dollars}$$
Problem 3
Ch. 4 — Maximum Voltage with a Safety Factor
A $2.2\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor rated at $1\ \text{W}$ is to be used following the rule of thumb that a resistor should be rated for at least twice the power it actually dissipates. What is the maximum voltage that can be applied across it while still meeting this safety factor?
Find the maximum allowable voltage $V_{max}$.
33.2 V
Step 1Apply the safety factor: $P_{allow} = 1\ \text{W} / 2 = 0.50\ \text{W}$.
Step 2Choose the formula linking power, voltage, and resistance: $P = V^2/R$.
Step 3Solve for voltage: $V = \sqrt{PR}$.
Step 4Substitute: $$V = \sqrt{0.50\ \text{W} \times 2200\ \Omega} = \sqrt{1100\ \text{V}^2}$$
Step 5State the result: $V_{max} = 33.2\ \text{V}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $R = 2.2\ \text{k}\Omega = 2200\ \Omega$, rating $P_{rated} = 1\ \text{W}$, safety factor $= 2$. The allowable dissipation is $$P_{allow} = \frac{P_{rated}}{2} = \frac{1\ \text{W}}{2} = 0.50\ \text{W}$$ With $P = V^2/R$, solve for $V$: $$V = \sqrt{P R} = \sqrt{0.50\ \text{W} \times 2200\ \Omega} = \sqrt{1100\ \text{V}^2} = 33.2\ \text{V}$$ Units: $\text{W} \cdot \Omega = (\text{V}^2/\Omega)\cdot\Omega = \text{V}^2$, so the square root is in volts. $V_{max} = 33.2\ \text{V}$.
Problem 4
Ch. 4 — Power from Voltage and Current
A small DC motor has $12\ \text{V}$ across it and draws $250\ \text{mA}$. Find the power it consumes.
Find the power $P$ in watts.
3.00 W
Step 1Convert the current to amperes: $250\ \text{mA} = 0.250\ \text{A}$.
Step 2Use $P = VI$ since voltage and current are known.
Step 3Substitute: $P = 12\ \text{V} \times 0.250\ \text{A}$.
Step 4State the result: $P = 3.00\ \text{W}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 12\ \text{V}$, $I = 250\ \text{mA} = 0.250\ \text{A}$. $$P = V I = 12\ \text{V} \times 0.250\ \text{A} = 3.00\ \text{W}$$ Units: $\text{V} \cdot \text{A} = \text{W}$.
Problem 5
Ch. 4 — Power from Current and Resistance
A current of $12\ \text{mA}$ flows through a $4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor. Find the power the resistor dissipates, in milliwatts.
Find the dissipated power $P$ in mW.
677 mW
Step 1Convert units: $I = 0.012\ \text{A}$, $R = 4700\ \Omega$.
Step 2Select $P = I^2 R$ since current and resistance are known.
Step 3Square the current first: $(0.012)^2 = 1.44 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}^2$.
Step 4Multiply by resistance: $$P = 1.44 \times 10^{-4} \times 4700 = 0.677\ \text{W}$$
Step 5Convert to milliwatts: $P = 677\ \text{mW}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $I = 12\ \text{mA} = 0.012\ \text{A}$, $R = 4.7\ \text{k}\Omega = 4700\ \Omega$. With current and resistance known, use $P = I^2 R$, squaring only the current: $$I^2 = (0.012\ \text{A})^2 = 1.44 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}^2$$ $$P = 1.44 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}^2 \times 4700\ \Omega = 0.677\ \text{W}$$ Converting, $P = 677\ \text{mW}$.
Problem 6
Ch. 4 — Battery Run Time Through a Regulator
A $12\ \text{V}$, $9.0\ \text{Ah}$ battery powers a voltage regulator that is $90\%$ efficient. The regulator delivers $3.3\ \text{V}$ at $2.0\ \text{A}$ to its load. Assuming the battery voltage stays at $12\ \text{V}$, find the theoretical run time of the battery.
Battery feeding a regulator that supplies a load
Find the theoretical run time $t$ in hours.
14.7 h
Step 1Find the output power: $P_{out} = 3.3\ \text{V} \times 2.0\ \text{A} = 6.6\ \text{W}$.
Step 2Use efficiency to find input power: $$P_{in} = \frac{6.6\ \text{W}}{0.90} = 7.33\ \text{W}$$
Step 3Find the current drawn from the battery: $I = 7.33\ \text{W} / 12\ \text{V} = 0.611\ \text{A}$.
Step 4Divide capacity by current: $$t = \frac{9.0\ \text{Ah}}{0.611\ \text{A}}$$
Step 5State the result: $t = 14.7\ \text{h}$, an upper bound in practice.
Worked Solution
Given: battery $12\ \text{V}$, $9.0\ \text{Ah}$; efficiency $\eta = 0.90$; load $3.3\ \text{V}$ at $2.0\ \text{A}$. Output power: $$P_{out} = 3.3\ \text{V} \times 2.0\ \text{A} = 6.6\ \text{W}$$ Input power from the battery: $$P_{in} = \frac{P_{out}}{\eta} = \frac{6.6\ \text{W}}{0.90} = 7.33\ \text{W}$$ Battery current: $$I_{batt} = \frac{P_{in}}{V_{batt}} = \frac{7.33\ \text{W}}{12\ \text{V}} = 0.611\ \text{A}$$ Run time: $$t = \frac{9.0\ \text{Ah}}{0.611\ \text{A}} = 14.7\ \text{h}$$
Problem 7
Ch. 4 — Battery Run Time
A $2.4\ \text{Ah}$ battery supplies a steady current of $60\ \text{mA}$. How many hours will it last, in theory?
Find the run time $t$ in hours.
40.0 h
Step 1Convert the current: $60\ \text{mA} = 0.060\ \text{A}$.
Step 2Use $t = \text{ampere-hours} \div \text{current}$.
Step 3Substitute: $t = 2.4\ \text{Ah} / 0.060\ \text{A}$.
Step 4State the result: $t = 40.0\ \text{h}$.
Worked Solution
Given: capacity $= 2.4\ \text{Ah}$, $I = 60\ \text{mA} = 0.060\ \text{A}$. $$t = \frac{\text{Ah}}{I} = \frac{2.4\ \text{Ah}}{0.060\ \text{A}} = 40.0\ \text{h}$$ The amperes cancel, leaving hours.
Problem 8
Ch. 4 — Power from Voltage and Resistance
A $4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor has $30\ \text{V}$ across it. Without calculating the current, find the power it dissipates in milliwatts.
Find the dissipated power $P$ in mW.
191 mW
Step 1Convert resistance: $4.7\ \text{k}\Omega = 4700\ \Omega$.
Step 2Select $P = V^2/R$ since voltage and resistance are known.
Step 3Square the voltage: $30^2 = 900\ \text{V}^2$.
Step 4Divide: $$P = \frac{900}{4700} = 0.191\ \text{W}$$
Step 5Convert: $P = 191\ \text{mW}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 30\ \text{V}$, $R = 4.7\ \text{k}\Omega = 4700\ \Omega$. Use $P = V^2/R$, squaring the voltage first: $$V^2 = (30\ \text{V})^2 = 900\ \text{V}^2$$ $$P = \frac{900\ \text{V}^2}{4700\ \Omega} = 0.191\ \text{W} = 191\ \text{mW}$$
Problem 9
Ch. 4 — Power Supply Efficiency
A power supply draws $150\ \text{W}$ from the wall and delivers $135\ \text{W}$ to its load. Find its efficiency.
Find the efficiency as a percentage.
90.0 %
Step 1Write the efficiency formula: $\eta = P_{out}/P_{in} \times 100\%$.
Step 2Substitute: $\eta = 135\ \text{W} / 150\ \text{W} \times 100\%$.
Step 3Simplify: $0.90 \times 100\%$.
Step 4State the result: $\eta = 90.0\%$.
Worked Solution
Given: $P_{in} = 150\ \text{W}$, $P_{out} = 135\ \text{W}$. $$\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\% = \frac{135\ \text{W}}{150\ \text{W}} \times 100\% = 90.0\%$$ The watts cancel, so efficiency is dimensionless.
Problem 10
Ch. 4 — Battery Energy from Ampere-Hours
A phone battery is rated $4.0\ \text{Ah}$ at $3.7\ \text{V}$. Find the energy it stores, in joules. Use $1\ \text{h} = 3600\ \text{s}$.
Find the stored energy $W$ in joules.
5.33e4 J
Step 1Recognize that ampere-hours measure charge, not energy; multiply by voltage.
Step 2Compute watt-hours: $W = 4.0\ \text{Ah} \times 3.7\ \text{V} = 14.8\ \text{Wh}$.
Step 3Use $1\ \text{Wh} = 3600\ \text{J}$.
Step 4Convert: $$W = 14.8 \times 3600 = 53\,280\ \text{J}$$
Step 5Round to 3 significant figures: $W = 5.33 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: capacity $= 4.0\ \text{Ah}$, $V = 3.7\ \text{V}$. Ampere-hours are charge, so multiply by voltage to get energy: $$W = 4.0\ \text{Ah} \times 3.7\ \text{V} = 14.8\ \text{Wh}$$ Convert watt-hours to joules ($1\ \text{Wh} = 1\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3600\ \text{J}$): $$W = 14.8\ \text{Wh} \times 3600\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{Wh}} = 53\,280\ \text{J} \approx 5.33 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$$
Problem 11
Ch. 4 — Kilowatt-Hours to Joules
A household appliance uses $3.2\ \text{kWh}$ of energy in a day. Express this energy in joules, using $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$.
Find the energy in joules.
1.15e7 J
Step 1Recall the conversion: $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$.
Step 2Multiply: $W = 3.2 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J} = 1.152 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J}$.
Step 3Round to 3 significant figures: $W = 1.15 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $W = 3.2\ \text{kWh}$ and $1\ \text{kWh} = 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$. $$W = 3.2\ \text{kWh} \times 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{kWh}} = 1.152 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J} \approx 1.15 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J}$$
Problem 12
Ch. 4 — Square-Law Scaling of Power
A fixed resistor dissipates $0.15\ \text{W}$ when $12\ \text{mA}$ flows through it. If the current increases to $30\ \text{mA}$ and the resistance stays the same, what power does it dissipate?
Find the new power $P_2$ in watts.
0.938 W
Step 1Note that with $R$ fixed, $P = I^2R$ means $P \propto I^2$.
Step 2Form the ratio: $$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{30}{12}\right)^2 = 6.25$$
Step 3Multiply: $P_2 = 6.25 \times 0.15\ \text{W}$.
Step 4State the result: $P_2 = 0.938\ \text{W}$ — 2.5 times the current gives 6.25 times the power.
Worked Solution
Given: $P_1 = 0.15\ \text{W}$ at $I_1 = 12\ \text{mA}$; $I_2 = 30\ \text{mA}$; $R$ constant. Since $P = I^2 R$ with $R$ fixed, power scales with the square of current: $$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{30\ \text{mA}}{12\ \text{mA}}\right)^2 = 2.5^2 = 6.25$$ $$P_2 = 6.25 \times 0.15\ \text{W} = 0.9375 \approx 0.938\ \text{W}$$ Check: $R = P_1/I_1^2 = 0.15/(0.012)^2 = 1042\ \Omega$, and $P_2 = (0.030)^2 \times 1042 = 0.938\ \text{W}$.
Problem 13
Ch. 4 — Heat Lost in a Power Supply
A laptop power adapter draws $120\ \text{W}$ from the wall and delivers $96\ \text{W}$ to the laptop. How much power becomes heat inside the adapter?
Find the power lost as heat in watts.
24.0 W
Step 1Recognize that input power equals output power plus heat.
Step 2Write $P_{heat} = P_{in} - P_{out}$.
Step 3Substitute: $P_{heat} = 120\ \text{W} - 96\ \text{W}$.
Step 4State the result: $P_{heat} = 24.0\ \text{W}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $P_{in} = 120\ \text{W}$, $P_{out} = 96\ \text{W}$. All input power leaves either as useful output or as heat: $$P_{heat} = P_{in} - P_{out} = 120\ \text{W} - 96\ \text{W} = 24.0\ \text{W}$$
Problem 14
Ch. 4 — Maximum Current from a Power Rating
A $2.2\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor is dissipating exactly $0.25\ \text{W}$. Find the current through it, in milliamperes.
Find the current $I$ in mA.
10.7 mA
Step 1Start from $P = I^2 R$ and solve for current: $I = \sqrt{P/R}$.
Step 2Substitute: $$I = \sqrt{\frac{0.25\ \text{W}}{2200\ \Omega}} = \sqrt{1.136 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}^2}$$
Step 3Evaluate: $I = 0.0107\ \text{A}$.
Step 4Convert: $I = 10.7\ \text{mA}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $P = 0.25\ \text{W}$, $R = 2200\ \Omega$. Rearrange $P = I^2R$: $$I = \sqrt{\frac{P}{R}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.25\ \text{W}}{2200\ \Omega}} = \sqrt{1.136 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}^2} = 0.0107\ \text{A}$$ Units: $\text{W}/\Omega = \text{A}^2$. Converting, $I = 10.7\ \text{mA}$.
Problem 15
Ch. 4 — Energy from Power and Time
A $40\ \text{W}$ soldering iron is left on for 15 minutes. How much energy does it use, in joules?
Find the energy $W$ in joules.
3.60e4 J
Step 1Convert time to seconds: $15\ \text{min} = 900\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Use $W = Pt$.
Step 3Substitute: $W = 40\ \text{W} \times 900\ \text{s}$.
Step 4State the result: $W = 3.60 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $P = 40\ \text{W}$, $t = 15\ \text{min} = 900\ \text{s}$. $$W = P t = 40\ \text{W} \times 900\ \text{s} = 36\,000\ \text{J} = 3.60 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$$ Units: $\text{W} \cdot \text{s} = (\text{J/s}) \cdot \text{s} = \text{J}$.
Problem 16
Ch. 4 — Input Power from Efficiency
A power supply that is $75\%$ efficient must deliver $60\ \text{W}$ to its load. How much power must it draw from the wall?
Find the required input power $P_{in}$ in watts.
80.0 W
Step 1Convert efficiency to a decimal: $75\% = 0.75$.
Step 2Rearrange the efficiency formula: $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$.
Step 3Substitute: $$P_{in} = \frac{60\ \text{W}}{0.75}$$
Step 4State the result: $P_{in} = 80.0\ \text{W}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $\eta = 75\% = 0.75$, $P_{out} = 60\ \text{W}$. Rearrange $\eta = P_{out}/P_{in}$: $$P_{in} = \frac{P_{out}}{\eta} = \frac{60\ \text{W}}{0.75} = 80.0\ \text{W}$$ The supply therefore produces $80.0 - 60 = 20\ \text{W}$ of heat.
Problem 17
Ch. 4 — Required Battery Capacity
A portable sensor draws a steady $350\ \text{mA}$ and must run for $8.0\ \text{h}$. What minimum ampere-hour capacity must its battery have, in theory?
Find the required capacity in ampere-hours.
2.80 Ah
Step 1Convert the current: $350\ \text{mA} = 0.350\ \text{A}$.
Step 2Use capacity $= I \times t$.
Step 3Substitute: $0.350\ \text{A} \times 8.0\ \text{h}$.
Step 4State the result: $2.80\ \text{Ah}$ (choose a larger battery in practice).
Worked Solution
Given: $I = 350\ \text{mA} = 0.350\ \text{A}$, $t = 8.0\ \text{h}$. Capacity is current times time: $$\text{Capacity} = I t = 0.350\ \text{A} \times 8.0\ \text{h} = 2.80\ \text{Ah}$$
Problem 18
Ch. 4 — Resistor Accidentally Across the Supply
A $68\ \Omega$ resistor $R_1$ rated at $\tfrac{1}{4}\ \text{W}$ is accidentally connected directly across a $9.0\ \text{V}$ supply $V_S$, with nothing else in the circuit. By what factor does the power it tries to dissipate exceed its rating?
Resistor R1 connected directly across the supply VS
Find the ratio of dissipated power to rated power.
4.76 (dimensionless)
Step 1Note that the full supply voltage appears across $R_1$.
Step 2Compute the dissipation: $$P = \frac{(9.0)^2}{68} = 1.19\ \text{W}$$
Step 3Compare with the rating: factor $= 1.19\ \text{W} / 0.25\ \text{W}$.
Step 4State the result: factor $= 4.76$, so the part is overloaded.
Worked Solution
Given: $R_1 = 68\ \Omega$, $P_{rated} = 0.25\ \text{W}$, $V_S = 9.0\ \text{V}$ appears entirely across $R_1$. $$P = \frac{V_S^2}{R_1} = \frac{(9.0\ \text{V})^2}{68\ \Omega} = \frac{81}{68} = 1.19\ \text{W}$$ $$\text{Factor} = \frac{P}{P_{rated}} = \frac{1.19\ \text{W}}{0.25\ \text{W}} = 4.76$$ The resistor is driven to nearly five times its rating and will overheat, discolor, and likely fail open.
Problem 19
Ch. 4 — Operating Time from Energy and Power
A $200\ \text{W}$ television used $0.90\ \text{kWh}$ of energy. For how many hours was it on?
Find the operating time $t$ in hours.
4.50 h
Step 1Convert power to kilowatts: $200\ \text{W} = 0.200\ \text{kW}$.
Step 2Rearrange $W = Pt$ to $t = W/P$.
Step 3Substitute: $t = 0.90\ \text{kWh} / 0.200\ \text{kW}$.
Step 4State the result: $t = 4.50\ \text{h}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $W = 0.90\ \text{kWh}$, $P = 200\ \text{W} = 0.200\ \text{kW}$. Rearrange $W = Pt$: $$t = \frac{W}{P} = \frac{0.90\ \text{kWh}}{0.200\ \text{kW}} = 4.50\ \text{h}$$
Problem 20
Ch. 4 — Current from Power and Voltage
A $100\ \text{W}$ lamp operates at $120\ \text{V}$. Find the current it draws.
Find the current $I$ in amperes.
0.833 A
Step 1Start from $P = VI$.
Step 2Solve for current: $I = P/V$.
Step 3Substitute: $I = 100\ \text{W} / 120\ \text{V}$.
Step 4State the result: $I = 0.833\ \text{A}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $P = 100\ \text{W}$, $V = 120\ \text{V}$. Rearrange $P = VI$: $$I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{100\ \text{W}}{120\ \text{V}} = 0.833\ \text{A}$$ Units: $\text{W}/\text{V} = \text{A}$.
